Foundation examination: Volumes1–4Economics core examination

Author-reviewed

Cumulative assessment · Volumes 1–4

Foundation examination and data practical

Connect a financial decision to a mathematical argument, an uncertainty model and a reproducible empirical calculation.

This assessment follows all four foundation volumes. Its purpose is to test whether you can choose and combine methods when the question no longer names the chapter. Two written forms, a practical analysis and oral transfer provide different kinds of evidence. The problems and datasets are original. Completing them does not establish expertise in the later economics, finance or research curriculum.

Rules and scoringForm AForm BData practicalOral transferCoverage and repair routes

Administration and advancement

First finish the chapters and assessment packages for economic and financial reasoning, mathematics, probability and statistical decisions, and data and computation. Their exercises, projects and delayed checks supply the wider coverage on which this cumulative assessment relies. A single examination samples capabilities; it cannot examine every theorem and boundary case in 48 chapters.

Take one written form in 180 minutes, with closed notes and solutions, a basic nonprogrammable calculator, and paper for derivations. No internet, code execution or assistance is needed for the written problems. Code or pseudocode may be written where requested. State the target and units, show the argument and check feasibility or assumptions. Give enough intermediate reasoning that a reviewer can distinguish a method error from a minor arithmetic slip.

Each form has four essential domains worth 25 points each, with five 5-point parts per domain. The written gate is 85/100 overall and at least 19/25 in every domain. The domain threshold rounds 75% of 25 upward to a whole point. Follow-through credit can recognize a correct subsequent method using an earlier wrong number; it cannot award points for a false interpretation or a missing condition. Equivalent valid methods earn credit. The supplied scoring is criterion based, not a percentile ranking.

Four essential domains
DomainEvidence requiredPrincipal foundation
D1 · Economic and financial reasoningDefine relevant alternatives, reconcile stocks and flows, and compare dated values using consistent units.Volume 1, supported by mathematical and computational checks.
D2 · Mathematical justificationDerive rather than merely report a solution; check existence, feasibility, boundaries and the conditions of a proof or approximation.Volume 2, with economic interpretations and exact numerical checks.
D3 · Uncertainty and decisionSpecify the probability or sampling law, quantify the relevant uncertainty and distinguish evidence from a loss-based decision.Volume 3, with explicit financial consequences and information sets.
D4 · Empirical and computational reasoningPreserve records, timing, populations and weights; audit calculations and separate descriptive, predictive and causal claims.Volume 4, drawing on all three earlier foundations.

Complete the open-resource data practical separately. A planning allowance of 3–5 hours covers analysis, checks and a concise report; it is not a measured completion-time norm. Its separate gate is 85/100 and 19/25 in each of the same four domains. The benchmark is a reference for checking your completed analysis. Running it unchanged and copying its outputs is not evidence that you can construct or defend the workflow.

Then attempt the four oral transfer tasks without notes. Allow 5–8 minutes each, with a short preparation sheet. The oral gate is 34/40 overall and at least 8/10 per task; 8 is the whole-point threshold above 75% of 10. An examiner should request one explanation in ordinary language and probe an assumption or changed input. Independent grading is preferable. If studying alone, record your reasoning before opening the answer and keep a discrepancy log; label that evidence as self-assessment.

A critical error in units, budget reconciliation, information availability, probability conditioning, causal identification or integrity requires a demonstrated repair even if a total passes. Record the mistaken inference, its consequence, the corrected argument and a fresh changed-input answer. Genuine disagreements over an open decision are resolved through its stated loss, assumptions and evidence, not conformity to a preferred opinion.

Reserve the other written form for reassessment after targeted remediation, preferably after a 7–14 day interval. If you already studied its solutions, it is practice rather than an unseen test; ask a reviewer to change inputs and verify the new solution before using it as transfer evidence. Keep the practical as a separate requirement. Do not average a failed essential domain away using a strong unrelated score. The time allowances, thresholds and suggested intervals are this library's design choices; they are not university requirements or empirically calibrated guarantees.

The solution panels are intentionally accessible for self-study and expand when printing. For supervised closed-note work, provide only the question sections and supply the solutions after collection. This HTML file is instructional material, not a secure examination system.

Foundation Form A — From a model to a defensible decision

Allow 180 minutes, closed notes and solutions, with a basic nonprogrammable calculator. Complete all four 25-point domains; each has five parts worth 5 points each. Show reasoning, dates and units. Exact expressions or correctly rounded decimals are acceptable. All firms, measurements, economic coefficients and probability laws below are original synthetic teaching cases. The stated rates and models are assumptions, not current market facts.

  1. D1. An investment, its alternative and its funding — 25 points

    A company can buy a machine for 500 USD now, at time 0. It would use an already owned room for two years. Without the project, the room would earn rental receipts of 54 USD at year 1 and 58.32 USD at year 2; those receipts are forgone if the project proceeds. Machine operations generate net cash receipts before financing of 324 USD at year 1 and 349.92 USD at year 2. The machine is sold for 116.64 USD at year 2. The room remains owned in either alternative; its later use is identical. An unrecoverable 40 USD feasibility study was paid before time 0 and is already reflected in the opening accounts.

    All future cash amounts are nominal USD paid at the stated year-ends. Assume annual inflation of 8%, an annual effective nominal project opportunity rate of 13.4%, and no omitted taxes, costs or cash flows. Treat these cash flows as stipulated for the valuation exercise. For funding, a bank offers a loan of exactly 300 USD at time 0, with 30 USD interest at each year-end and all 300 USD principal repaid at year 2. Its financing cash flows are separate from the project-versus-rental comparison.

    Immediately before the new loan and purchase, the company's balance sheet contains cash 1,000 USD and the room at a book value of 300 USD, debt 400 USD and equity 900 USD. There are no other assets or obligations in this snapshot. At time 0, record the new machine at its purchase cost; no time has elapsed for depreciation. A binding cash policy requires at least 850 USD immediately after initiating the project.

    1. Construct the three dated incremental project-versus-rental cash flows before financing. Explain the treatment of the old study, the forgone rent and the room's book value.
    2. Derive the effective real discount rate. Compute NPV using both nominal cash flows and time-0 purchasing-power cash flows, and explain why the answers agree. State the conditional valuation decision.
    3. List the loan's cash flows separately. Add them to the incremental project cash flows to obtain the cash-flow sequence after this financing. Explain why loan proceeds are not operating revenue, principal repayment is not an operating expense, and this new sequence should not automatically be discounted at the project's unfinanced opportunity rate.
    4. Reconcile the company's time-0 balance sheet after receiving the loan and buying the machine. Show cash, other assets, debt, equity and the balance-sheet identity. Does borrowing itself create profit or raise book equity here?
    5. Check the 850 USD cash policy, quantify any funding shortfall, and give a feasible-to-evaluate next step without assuming that further finance is already available. Explain why positive NPV alone does not establish liquidity feasibility or an unconditional recommendation.

  2. D2. Workload equilibrium and constrained allocation — 25 points

    A delivery operation's normalized steady workload u is required to solve u = T(u), where

    T(u) = (1 + u²)/4,   u ∈ [0, 1].

    After determining its fixed point u*, management allocates continuous delivery blocks x and y, with x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 and x + y ≤ c, where 0 ≤ c ≤ 4. The objective is

    F(x,y;u*) = (4 + u*)x + (2 + u*)y − (x² + y²)/2.

    The numerical quantities x, y and c count standardized delivery blocks per day; F is measured in hundreds of USD per day, with the displayed coefficients incorporating those units. Workload u is dimensionless and is held fixed when capacity c changes. No integer restrictions are imposed. Define V(c) as the maximum attainable F at capacity c.

    1. Show that T maps [0,1] into itself and has a Lipschitz constant q = 1/2 there. Prove existence and uniqueness of a fixed point in this interval, checking the conditions of any theorem used. Obtain its exact value and exclude the other algebraic root.
    2. Starting at u₀ = 0, calculate u₁, u₂ and u₃. Derive a bound on |u₃ − u*| from the latest increment and q. Does that bound certify an error below 0.001? Using the bound qⁿ|u₁ − u₀|/(1 − q), find the smallest n for which this particular a priori bound is below 0.001; do not confuse this with the smallest n having that actual error.
    3. Explain why the capacity constraint binds at an optimum for 0 < c ≤ 4. Substitute y = c − x, derive the one-variable derivative, and find the unique optimal allocations at c = 1 and c = 4. Check the relevant boundary rather than applying an interior formula outside its domain.
    4. Derive x*(c), y*(c) and V(c) for the entire interval 0 ≤ c ≤ 4, identifying the capacity at which the active boundary changes. Show that V and its first derivative agree across that transition.
    5. Give V′(4) from the left and its units. Approximate V(4) using u₃, and propagate your part (b) workload-error bound into a bound on this value error, in both the objective's units and USD per day. Does this arithmetic certificate establish that the economic coefficients are accurate?

  3. D3. Buying a signal and interpreting statistical evidence — 25 points

    A machine is in a fault state H with prior probability 1/5 and a sound state L otherwise. A risk-neutral operator can service it now or leave it alone. Service costs 40 USD in either state and prevents all fault damage. Leaving it alone costs 160 USD if H and zero if L. These are complete losses over the decision horizon; both actions are feasible.

    A diagnostic report is positive with probability 3/4 conditional on H and 1/4 conditional on L. It is negative otherwise. The report does not change the state or service effectiveness. If acquired, it is observed before the service decision. Later fee questions assume any report invoice must be paid regardless of the subsequent service action, and no liquidity constraint binds.

    1. Construct the four joint probabilities for state and report. Find the positive-report probability and both posterior fault probabilities. Identify which probability is a signal likelihood and which is a posterior.
    2. For a fault belief p, derive the service threshold, including the equality case. Find the best action and expected loss without a report, and the best action after each report.
    3. Calculate expected loss under the optimal free-report policy. Find the gross expected value of sample information and of perfect information, measured as reductions in expected loss. Verify their ordering and explain why a favorable report's conditional loss is not the ex ante value of acquiring the report.
    4. The vendor charges 28 USD only when the report is positive and zero otherwise, irrespective of whether service is chosen. Compute the expected invoice and total expected loss if the report is bought. Decide whether to buy and derive the largest positive-report-only fee that leaves the operator indifferent. Does the realized invoice change the optimal service action after observing a report under these assumptions?
    5. Separately, a preregistered pilot observes 36 iid normal cost savings with unknown fixed mean μ and known standard deviation 12 USD. Its sample mean is 5 USD. Construct a two-sided 95% confidence interval using z0.975 = 1.96, and derive its repeated-sampling coverage from the normal pivot. Evaluate the claim that this means a 95% posterior probability that μ lies in the realized interval or that μ exceeds a 4 USD cost threshold. Contrast with the explicit Bayesian probabilities in part (a).

  4. D4. A historical panel, a fitted line and a causal claim — 25 points

    Three firms A, B and C are active throughout this case. For each firm-month, y is monthly output in hundreds of completed units. Its x is an automation dose, measured in normalized hours per working day: A has x = 0, B has x = 1 and C has x = 2 in every month. Doses and firm identities are known before forecast origins. The table contains successive releases; each value becomes available at the end of its release date. No row is a forecast. The original analysis freezes inputs at the end of 15 March 2024 and fits y = a + bx by unweighted least squares on January and February only.

    Source release history for the training panel
    FirmReference monthRelease datexy
    A2024-012024-02-1002
    A2024-012024-03-2004
    B2024-012024-02-1014
    C2024-012024-02-1025
    A2024-022024-03-1003
    B2024-022024-03-1014
    C2024-022024-03-1026

    Two candidates are frozen from that same March snapshot: the fitted line and the constant forecast equal to the training mean. Their April forecasts are recorded on 15 March. After April labels arrive, choose the candidate with smaller April MSE once on 11 May, with ties favoring the constant, then use its unchanged rule for June. The selected rule's June forecast is recorded on 11 May. Do not refit either candidate or change the selection rule in the stated protocol. The following values are supplied with hindsight.

    Validation and final outcomes, in hundreds of units
    Reference monthRoleRelease dateA outputB outputC output
    2024-04validation2024-05-10357
    2024-06final2024-07-10444

    For a separate causal interpretation, A is a small firm; B and C are large firms. Size was measured before automation. All large firms in the target population use a strictly positive dose; no large firm's zero-dose outcome is observed. The target is the effect, for large firms, of their current dose compared with zero. No random assignment or exchangeability assumption has been supplied.

    1. State the release-history key and the selected panel key. Describe a deterministic selection rule for the 15 March information set, list the six selected y values in month-then-firm order, and give A's January-to-February output change using that vintage. Explain why both A–January rows must not be treated as separate firm-month observations.
    2. Derive a and b from centered sums. List the six residuals in the same order, verify both normal equations, and calculate SSE. State what the residual equations establish about this fitted sample.
    3. Calculate both candidates' April MSEs and select the rule at 11 May. Calculate both June MSEs, identify the earliest full final-score date and state which score evaluates the original selection protocol. Include squared units.
    4. A script first takes the latest release for every firm-month without filtering on the historical cutoff. It then labels the resulting fit's April score “performance of a 15 March forecast.” Diagnose the error and give a minimal corrected algorithm, including duplicate-key and missing-coverage checks. Would using the 20 March revision for a newly declared June forecast made on 11 May automatically be look-ahead leakage? Explain what must change in the analysis record.
    5. Evaluate the claim that the fitted slope identifies the target causal effect because residuals are orthogonal to x. Identify the missing support cell and what a linear zero-dose prediction for large firms adds. Explain why repeating each firm's observations over months does not by itself establish exchangeability or independent sampling evidence.
Foundation Form A solutions and point allocation

Each part is worth 5 points, with 25 per domain and 100 overall. Award consistent arithmetic follow-through when the later method is correct. A wrong information set, counterfactual, unit, feasibility claim or probability interpretation does not earn its associated reasoning point. Equivalent valid arguments receive credit.

  1. D1 solutions

    1. Before financing, incremental flows at years (0,1,2) are (−500, 324 − 54, 349.92 + 116.64 − 58.32) = (−500, 270, 408.24) nominal USD. The study is sunk: neither present alternative recovers or changes its past payment. Rent is a future opportunity cost even though the room is owned. Its 300 USD book value is a stock in the accounts, not an additional dated cash outflow; the room is retained in both alternatives. Including that book value as a new cost would double-count an irrelevant common holding rather than value a stated forgone use.

      Scoring: three dated flows 2; sunk-study treatment 1; rental opportunity cost 1; book-value/common-asset distinction 1.

    2. Consistency requires (1 + rnom) = (1 + π)(1 + rreal), so rreal = 1.134/1.08 − 1 = 0.05. Deflating at each date gives 270/1.08 = 250 and 408.24/1.08² = 350 time-0-purchasing-power USD. Thus

      NPV = −500 + 270/1.134 + 408.24/1.134²
      = −500 + 250/1.05 + 350/1.05² = 500/9 ≈ 55.555556 time-0 USD.

      The equality follows period by period because 1.134ᵗ = 1.08ᵗ1.05ᵗ. Positive NPV favors the project over renting under these complete incremental flows and the stipulated opportunity rate, subject to feasibility and the stated model. Discounting nominal amounts at 5% would overstate this valuation.

      Scoring: real-rate derivation 1; correctly dated real flows 1; nominal NPV 1; real NPV and consistency explanation 1; conditional decision 1.

    3. The loan sequence is (+300, −30, −330) USD, the final amount containing 30 interest and 300 principal. Adding it yields (−200, 240, 78.24) USD after this financing. Proceeds create both cash and an obligation, not sales or operating profit. Principal repayment reduces cash and debt, not an operating expense; interest is a financing cost. The asset-level rate was specified for the unfinanced incremental comparison. Financing changes the cash-flow claim and can change its appropriate required return, so inserting debt cash flows into the old NPV formula without a coherent financing/claim valuation would answer an unstated question. No equity discount rate is supplied.

      Scoring: loan sequence 1; combined sequence 1; proceeds classification 1; principal/interest classification 1; discount-rate/claim consistency 1.

    4. Cash becomes 1,000 + 300 − 500 = 800 USD. Other assets are the room 300 and new machine 500, so total assets are 1,600. Debt is 400 + 300 = 700 and equity remains 900. The identity is 800 + 300 + 500 = 700 + 900. The loan increases assets and liabilities together; purchasing the machine swaps cash for an asset. Neither time-0 transaction creates profit or book equity here. The already expensed study is not deducted again.

      Scoring: cash 1; other assets/total 1; debt and equity 1; balanced identity 1; no profit/equity creation or double counting 1.

    5. Cash 800 is 50 USD below the required 850, so the specified funding arrangement fails the policy. A proposed next step is to seek and evaluate an additional 50 USD equity contribution, renegotiated funding, a lower time-0 cost or a delayed project; none is assumed already feasible. Any additional loan would require new debt-service and liability calculations, and additional equity is not sales revenue. Positive NPV compares discounted complete flows under a rate/model; it does not supply cash at a required date, authorize overriding a constraint or establish that real forecasts and alternatives equal the stipulated values. Under the currently supplied arrangement the project cannot proceed while honoring the policy.

      Scoring: policy failure 1; shortfall 1; conditional practical next step 1; liquidity versus value distinction 1; qualified recommendation/model scope 1.

  2. D2 solutions

    1. On [0,1], T is increasing and T([0,1]) = [1/4,1/2] ⊂ [0,1]. It is continuously differentiable, with T′(u) = u/2 between 0 and 1/2; the mean value theorem gives |T(u) − T(v)| ≤ (1/2)|u − v|. The interval is closed in complete ℝ, hence complete and nonempty, so the contraction theorem supplies a fixed point. Alternatively, the continuous function T(u) − u is positive at 0 and negative at 1, so the intermediate value theorem supplies existence. If u and v are fixed, |u − v| ≤ (1/2)|u − v| forces equality, proving uniqueness. The equation is u² − 4u + 1 = 0, with roots 2 ± √3; only u* = 2 − √3 ≈ 0.267949192 lies in [0,1].

      Scoring: self-map 1; global Lipschitz argument 1; valid existence conditions 1; uniqueness argument 1; root and excluded alternative 1.

    2. u₁ = 1/4, u₂ = 17/64 = 0.265625 and u₃ = 4385/16384 ≈ 0.267639160. Iteration increments contract: |uk+1 − uk| ≤ q|uk − uk−1|. Since the iterates converge to u*, telescoping the tail and summing its geometric bound gives |uₙ − u*| ≤ [q/(1 − q)]|uₙ − un−1|. At n = 3 this is 33/16384 ≈ 0.002014160, which does not certify an error below 0.001, although the actual error is smaller. The stated a priori bound is (1/2)ⁿ(1/4)/(1/2) = 2−n−1. It is 1/512 at n = 8 and 1/1024 at n = 9, so 9 is the first n passing that bound. This is a conservative certificate, not a claim that nine iterations are necessary in fact.

      Scoring: three iterates 1; geometric-tail derivation 1; latest-step bound 1; certification interpretation 1; smallest n for the specified a priori bound 1.

    3. The feasible triangle is nonempty and compact, and F is continuous, so a maximum exists. If x + y < c ≤ 4, then x < 4 and Fx = 4 + u* − x > 0: slightly increasing x is feasible and raises F. Thus capacity binds for positive c. With y = c − x and 0 ≤ x ≤ c, the derivative is 2 + c − 2x and the second derivative is −2. The stationary candidate is x = (c + 2)/2, but it must lie in [0,c]. For c = 1 that candidate is 1.5 > 1, the derivative is positive throughout [0,1], and the unique maximum is (x,y) = (1,0). For c = 4 the candidate (3,1) is feasible and is the unique global maximum by strict concavity. Both comparisons use the boundary and the full feasible interval.

      Scoring: existence/binding argument 1; derivative and curvature 1; c = 1 corner 1; c = 4 interior allocation 1; feasibility/global uniqueness justification 1.

    4. For 0 ≤ c ≤ 2 the stationary x would exceed c (or equal it at 2), so x* = c and y* = 0. For 2 ≤ c ≤ 4, x* = (c + 2)/2 and y* = (c − 2)/2. Substitution gives

      V(c) = (4 + u*)c − c²/2,   0 ≤ c ≤ 2;
      V(c) = 1 + (3 + u*)c − c²/4,   2 ≤ c ≤ 4.

      The zero-y boundary stops binding beyond c = 2. Both value formulas give 6 + 2u* at 2. Their derivatives are 4 + u* − c and 3 + u* − c/2, both equal to 2 + u* at 2. Thus V and V′ join continuously, although their second derivatives differ. At c = 0 the sole feasible allocation is (0,0) and V = 0, consistent with the first formula.

      Scoring: corner allocation range 1; interior allocation range/transition 1; first value formula 1; second value formula 1; value/derivative matching and zero-capacity boundary 1.

    5. The left marginal value at 4 is 3 + u* − 4/2 = 1 + u* = 3 − √3 ≈ 1.267949192 hundreds of USD per day per added block per day. It describes a local capacity change from within the stated range. V(4) = 9 + 4u* = 17 − 4√3 ≈ 10.071796770 hundreds of USD per day. Using u₃ gives 9 + 4u₃ = 41249/4096 ≈ 10.070556641. Since value depends linearly on u with coefficient 4 here, its error is at most 4(33/16384) = 33/4096 ≈ 0.008056641 hundreds of USD per day, or 0.805664063 USD per day. This controls the error introduced by the approximate workload within this stipulated model. It supplies no bound on misspecified demand, costs or other economic coefficients.

      Scoring: marginal value and one-sided scope 1; its units 1; approximate V(4) 1; propagated bound in both unit systems 1; arithmetic/model distinction 1.

  3. D3 solutions

    1. The joint masses are P(H,+) = (1/5)(3/4) = 3/20, P(H,−) = 1/20, P(L,+) = (4/5)(1/4) = 1/5 and P(L,−) = 3/5. Therefore P(+) = 7/20 and P(−) = 13/20. Bayes gives P(H | +) = (3/20)/(7/20) = 3/7 and P(H | −) = (1/20)/(13/20) = 1/13. The sensitivity 3/4 is P(+ | H), a report likelihood conditional on the state; it is not the posterior fault probability after a positive report.

      Scoring: four-cell joint law 1; report probabilities 1; positive posterior 1; negative posterior 1; likelihood/posterior direction 1.

    2. Service has loss 40; no service has expected loss 160p. Service is preferred when 40 < 160p, or p > 1/4; at equality both actions tie. Without a report p = 1/5, so leave the machine alone with expected loss 32 USD rather than 40. After a positive report p = 3/7 > 1/4, so service; after a negative report p = 1/13 < 1/4, so do not service. These minimize expected money losses under the stated risk-neutral objective.

      Scoring: expected losses/threshold 2; equality case 1; prior action/loss 1; both report actions 1.

    3. The free-report policy incurs 40 USD whenever positive and fault damage only in the joint event (H,−). Thus expected loss is (7/20)40 + (1/20)160 = 14 + 8 = 22 USD. Equivalently average conditional losses 40 and 160/13 using report probabilities. Gross EVSI = 32 − 22 = 10 USD. Perfect information services only in H, producing expected loss (1/5)40 = 8 USD and EVPI = 32 − 8 = 24 USD. Hence 0 ≤ 10 ≤ 24: a report can be ignored, while knowing the state can do at least as well. The conditional loss 40 after a positive report is neither an improvement over the optimal prior policy nor an average over possible reports; information value is the ex ante reduction relative to the best no-report action.

      Scoring: free-report expected loss 1; EVSI 1; perfect-information loss/EVPI 1; ordering and reason 1; ex ante versus conditional distinction 1.

    4. The expected invoice is (7/20)28 = 49/5 = 9.8 USD. Total expected loss is 22 + 9.8 = 31.8 USD, below the no-report 32 by 0.2, so buy under the stipulated objective and feasibility. If the positive-only fee is f, indifference requires 22 + (7/20)f = 32, giving f = 200/7 ≈ 28.571429 USD. Comparing the full conditional invoice 28 directly with EVSI 10 would ignore its probability of payment. Once the report is observed, the invoice is owed regardless of service, so it adds the same realized loss to both actions and does not change their ranking. A fee conditional on service, a binding liquidity constraint or a different risk objective would require a new calculation.

      Scoring: expected fee 1; total expected loss and purchase 1; indifference fee 1; correct contingent-fee comparison 1; unchanged conditional action and scope 1.

    5. SE = 12/√36 = 2 USD and the interval is 5 ± 1.96(2) = [1.08, 8.92] USD. Under the stipulated iid normal model, Z = (X̄ − μ)/(12/√36) is exactly standard normal for every fixed μ. Therefore Pμ(|Z| ≤ 1.96) ≈ 0.95, which is equivalent to the random interval [X̄ − 1.96·2, X̄ + 1.96·2] covering μ. The small approximation here comes from rounding the normal quantile to 1.96, not from a central-limit approximation. Once the data are fixed, this frequentist statement does not assign posterior mass to the realized interval or to μ > 4. The interval also contains 4. A posterior requires a prior and likelihood for μ; part (a) had an explicitly supplied state prior and report likelihood, which licensed its Bayesian probabilities.

      Scoring: SE and interval 2; pivot/coverage derivation 2; posterior and cost-threshold contrast 1.

  4. D4 solutions

    1. The source-history key is (firm, reference month, release date); the selected panel key is (firm, reference month). Validate uniqueness at the source key, retain releases no later than 15 March, then choose the greatest remaining release date separately for each required firm-month. Check that all three firms and both months remain. In January A/B/C order then February A/B/C order, selected y values are (2,4,5,3,4,6). A's calendar-month change is 3 − 2 = 1 hundred units. Its revision to January 4 was unavailable on 15 March. Counting both January versions as observations duplicates one firm-month and includes future information; a revision is not another firm or another production month.

      Scoring: both keys 1; filter-then-select rule 1; selected values 1; correctly vintaged change 1; duplicate-version explanation 1.

    2. x̄ = 1 and ȳ = 4. The centered x sum of squares is 1 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 = 4. The centered cross-product sum is 2 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 2 = 6. Hence b = 6/4 = 3/2 and a = 4 − 3/2 = 5/2. Fitted values in each month are (5/2,4,11/2), and residuals are (−1/2,0,−1/2,1/2,0,1/2). Their sum is zero; their x-weighted sum is −1 + 1 = 0. SSE = 4(1/4) = 1 squared hundred-unit, or 10,000 completed-units squared. These are the least-squares projection normal equations for this fitting sample. They establish sample residual orthogonality and, with distinct x values, a unique minimizing line; they do not identify a causal effect or prove future prediction accuracy.

      Scoring: means/centered sums 1; coefficients 1; residual vector 1; both normal equations 1; SSE units and projection scope 1.

    3. For April y = (3,5,7), line errors are (1/2,1,3/2), giving MSE (1/4 + 1 + 9/4)/3 = 7/6. Constant forecasts are all 4, with errors (−1,1,3), giving MSE (1 + 1 + 9)/3 = 11/3. April's labels are released on 10 May, so the 11 May selection can choose the line. For June y = (4,4,4), line errors are (3/2,0,−3/2), giving MSE 3/2; the constant's MSE is zero. All these losses are in squared hundreds of output units; multiplication by 10,000 converts to completed-units squared. June's full score becomes available after the end-of-day release on 10 July. The original protocol's final score is 3/2 because it selected the line. Choosing the constant after seeing June would use the final outcomes for selection, so zero would no longer be an untouched evaluation of that original protocol.

      Scoring: April MSEs 1; selection and availability 1; June MSEs 1; score date and squared units 1; original-protocol score and reselection limit 1.

    4. The unconstrained latest selector uses A's January revision released on 20 March, five days after the claimed forecast origin. Its historical forecast is infeasible even though the reference month is January. A corrected algorithm validates the unique (firm,month,release) keys and dates; filters release ≤ cutoff; chooses the maximum eligible release within each (firm,month); and verifies the selected keys equal the required January–February three-firm grid, failing on duplicates or uncovered active records rather than inventing values. Preserve original bytes, cutoff, definitions, selection code and the resulting model/forecast log. The revision is available on 11 May, so using it in a genuinely new June forecast is not automatically look-ahead. It would, however, be a new declared fitting procedure, not the unchanged March-frozen rule specified here. Preserve both versions and origins, state when the new rule was chosen, and evaluate it on outcomes not yet used in its selection. Do not rewrite the original March forecast or silently replace its score.

      Scoring: precise unavailable-version error 1; cutoff before per-key maximum 1; duplicate/coverage checks 1; legitimate later use distinguished from historical leakage 1; preserved versions/protocol and evaluation boundary 1.

    5. The missing cell is large firms at dose zero. Small A supplies a zero-dose observation, but it is not by itself a valid no-automation counterfactual for large B/C. Extending the pooled line to zero for large firms adds a functional-form/transport assumption across size and dose; residual orthogonality cannot supply it. A causal interpretation also needs a well-defined intervention, consistency/noninterference and an assignment or adjustment argument establishing the relevant counterfactual comparisons. No such exchangeability has been supplied, and the stipulated target lacks observed zero-dose support among large firms. Repeated months give more rows under the same assignments, not the missing untreated large-firm outcomes. Persistent firm shocks can also make their rows dependent, so six rows do not automatically behave like six iid draws. More observations or exact computation cannot by themselves repair the identification gap.

      Scoring: missing target support cell 1; role of pooled extrapolation 1; residual orthogonality versus causal assumptions 1; repeated rows do not supply counterfactuals 1; dependence/independent-evidence limitation 1.

Method routes: opportunity cost, balance sheets, dated value, nominal and real quantities, constrained optimization, value sensitivity, contraction proofs and error bounds, Bayes, confidence coverage, loss-based decisions, information value, release vintages, keys and coverage, projection, causal support, validation timing, and panel dependence.

Form B — Reconcile, certify and challenge the claim

100 points; 180 minutes; closed notes and solutions; basic nonprogrammable calculator. There are four essential domains, each worth 25 points through five parts worth 5 points each. Show the reasoning, state units and distinguish exact results from approximations. Exact fractions, powers and square-root expressions are acceptable. No code execution or external information is required. All businesses, records, populations and mechanisms below are original synthetic teaching constructions.

  1. D1 — Earnings, liquidity and financing, 25 points.

    A business uses the following simplified accrual rules: recognize the full sale as revenue, expense the recorded cost of goods sold, expense wages, depreciation and interest, and treat loan principal and owner distributions as financing rather than expenses. For this exercise classify interest paid as an operating cash flow. There are no taxes, new borrowing, owner contributions, equipment purchases, write-offs or other transactions.

    Opening stocks, all in USD on the same date
    ItemAmount
    Cash200
    Receivables120
    Inventory180
    Equipment, net500
    Supplier payables100
    Bank principal owed300
    Equity600
    All transactions and recognition entries during the following month
    EventAmount and timing
    SaleRevenue 160; inventory cost consumed 100; cash collected now 60, remainder on credit
    Old receivable collected80 cash; no new sale
    Inventory purchased140; paid 40 cash, remainder on supplier credit
    Supplier payment70 cash against amounts owed
    Wages30 expense, all paid in cash
    Depreciation20 equipment expense, no cash payment
    Bank principal payment40 cash
    Interest6 expense, all paid in cash
    Owner distribution14 cash

    Parts (d)–(e) concern a separate financing choice, not an extra transaction in the preceding month. A supplier permits an invoice to be settled for 900 USD now or 1000 USD exactly three months later. A bank will lend exactly 900 USD now, with no fees and no interim payments, quoting a nominal annual rate of 24% compounded monthly; the balance is repaid after three months. Alternatively, 900 USD of available internal cash could be used now. If retained, that cash would earn a certain effective three-month return of 5%. All choices are feasible, have the same goods received, and have no tax, default or liquidity differences.

    1. Calculate the month's accrual profit. Explain why collecting the old receivable is not another sale and why bank principal and the owner distribution do not reduce this profit. (5)
    2. Calculate all seven closing stocks in the opening table. Reconcile assets with liabilities plus equity without inserting a balancing item. (5)
    3. Calculate operating, investing and financing cash flows under the stated classification. Independently bridge accrual profit to operating cash flow using depreciation and changes in receivables, inventory and payables. Reconcile the cash-stock change. (5)
    4. Calculate the supplier's implicit effective three-month financing rate when the early payment is forgone. Calculate the bank's monthly and effective three-month rates, three-month repayment and effective annual rate. Why is the supplier's 10% discount off the later invoice not its financing rate on the amount advanced? (5)
    5. Compare all three financing choices by equivalent costs at the three-month date, including the opportunity cost of internal cash. Choose the cheapest under the assumptions and explain why “internal cash carries no cost because no interest invoice arrives” is wrong. (5)
  2. D2 — An allocation with a verifiable certificate, 25 points.

    Two divisible activities x and y, measured in the same activity unit, share capacity b. The loss is f(x,y)=(x−4)²+2(y−3)² in squared activity units. Define V(b) as the minimum of f over x≥0, y≥0 and x+y≤b. Begin with b=4. Use the minimization convention L=f+λ(x+y−b), λ≥0, retaining x,y≥0 in the domain when defining the dual lower bound. The activities and loss are a stipulated mathematical model, not an estimated causal relationship.

    1. Show that the b=4 problem has an attained unique global minimizer. Identify the properties of the feasible set and of f that establish existence and uniqueness; a first-order equation by itself is insufficient. (5)
    2. Solve for the minimizing activities and a valid capacity multiplier. Verify feasibility, stationarity with the nonnegativity multipliers, complementary slackness and the attained loss. (5)
    3. Complete the squares in L at λ=4 to compute the dual value. Use weak duality to certify the candidate globally. For the feasible candidate (1,3), calculate the primal–dual gap and explain exactly what error it bounds. (5)
    4. Keep λ=4 and derive a lower bound for V(b) at another nonnegative capacity b. Find the exact optima and values at b=0 and b=8. Compare them with this bound and explain why the old multiplier is not an exact finite-change formula. (5)
    5. Suppose capacity instead follows the deterministic update bt+1=2+bt/2, with b0=0 and integer t≥0. Derive its equilibrium and exact path, establish stability and nonnegativity, and find the first date with |bt−4|≤1/8 activity unit. State what assumption makes this path calculation applicable. (5)
  3. D3 — Sampling, evidence and decisions, 25 points.

    A fixed population consists of four account adjustments, (0,2,5,9) USD. Select two distinct accounts uniformly without replacement; every unordered pair is equally likely. For parts (a)–(c), randomness comes from the selection design, not from treating these four fixed values as estimated parameters.

    1. List all six possible sample means. Derive the mean and variance of the sample mean by exact enumeration, with units. (5)
    2. Order the two selected accounts randomly and call their values X1,X2. Find each draw's variance and their covariance. Reconstruct the sample-mean variance and compare it with two independent draws with replacement. Explain the dependence mechanism. (5)
    3. A null model specifies exactly the four listed population values and this sampling design. The observed selected pair is (5,9). For the predeclared upper-tail statistic “sample mean,” find the exact p-value Pnull(mean≥observed mean). Would the rule p≤α reject at α=0.20 or α=0.05? Give the actual null rejection probability of the α=0.20 rule, and explain why the p-value is not a posterior probability of the null. (5)
    4. In a separate decision, final wealth is 9 or 25 USD with equal probability. Utility is u(w)=√[w/(1 USD)] on positive wealth. Calculate expected wealth, expected utility, certainty-equivalent wealth and risk premium. Compare the lottery with certain wealth 16 USD under this utility and under risk neutrality. (5)
    5. For another experiment, independent fair signs ε1,ε2 produce cumulative gains M0=0, M1=ε1, M2=ε1+ε2 USD. Stop at T=1 if ε1=1; otherwise stop at T=2. Enumerate the stopped gains and their expectation. Compare with a hindsight report that records max(M1,M2) after both signs are known. Explain the stopping-time distinction and whether bounded optional stopping has been contradicted. (5)
  4. D4 — Data meaning survives the computation, 25 points.

    Four firm records contain a monthly service fee. A proposed target population consists of 1/4 small firms and 3/4 large firms. The analyst proposes using the observed within-group means as estimates of the corresponding target means. A separate directory contains one row per listed tag; each comma-separated tag below becomes a distinct directory row with that firm's ID.

    Original analytical records and one-to-many directory tags
    IDGroupFee, USDTags
    F1small0K,L
    F2small2K
    F3small4K
    F4large12K,L,M
    1. Calculate the unweighted four-firm mean, the two group means and the proposed population-weighted mean. Explain the additional within-group assumption needed for the last calculation to represent the target population rather than merely a reweighted description. (5)
    2. Inner-join every analytical row to all its directory tags on firm ID. Calculate the resulting row count and naive mean fee. Now apply the target group proportions to the joined group means: does that restore the original proposed target estimate? Explain the necessary grain-preserving repair. (5)
    3. Using the original four observations with equal firm weights, construct a density histogram with bins [0,3), [3,6), [6,15], including the last endpoint. Give counts, heights, areas and axis units. Does the resulting area distribution represent the target population's group weights from part (a)? (5)
    4. A separate ledger contains exact integer cents [253+3, −(253+2)]. In the declared binary64 rounding environment, converting these entries to float stores [253+4, −(253+2)]. Calculate the exact original sum and the exact sum of the stored values; separate conversion and subsequent summation error. Would an otherwise exact summation of the stored floats repair the result? Give one repair and one economic-data issue that exact arithmetic cannot settle. (5)
    5. Finally, let a fair binary U determine D=U. Two candidate structural models are A: Y(d)=50−4d and B: Y(d)=50−10U+6d, in USD. For each model list the observed (D,Y) pairs and its average treatment effect. Can perfect held-out prediction by 50−4D under the unchanged observation mechanism choose between these causal models? State why intervening on D asks a different question. (5)
Form B complete solutions and scoring

Each part totals 5 points. Give method credit for a consistently carried arithmetic slip, but withhold interpretation points for a wrong target, information set or unit. Equivalent valid derivations receive credit. The written mastery gate is 85/100 and at least 19/25 in each domain; these are library design choices. Critical errors require remediation even when the numerical total passes.

  1. D1.

    (a) Profit is 160−100−30−20−6=4 USD. The old receivable collection exchanges a claim for cash; its sale was already recognized. Principal repayment reduces cash and a liability rather than consuming a current-period service, while the owner distribution reduces cash and equity after profit. Neither is an expense under the supplied rules. Scoring: 2 complete profit calculation; 1 old receivable; 1 principal; 1 distribution.

    (b) Closing cash is 200+60+80−40−70−30−40−6−14=140. Receivables are 120+100−80=140; inventory is 180+140−100=220; net equipment is 500−20=480. Supplier payables are 100+100−70=130; bank principal is 300−40=260; equity is 600+4−14=590, all USD. Assets total 140+140+220+480=980 USD, matching liabilities 130+260=390 plus equity590. Opening assets1000 similarly equal liabilities400 plus equity600. Scoring: 1 cash; 1 receivables/inventory; 1 equipment; 1 liabilities/equity; 1 closing identity.

    (c) Direct operating cash flow is 60+80−40−70−30−6=−6 USD. Investing flow is zero; financing flow is −40−14=−54 USD. For the independent bridge, receivables rise20, inventory rises40 and payables rise30, so operating cash flow is profit4 + depreciation20 −20 −40 +30=−6. Depreciation is added back because it reduced profit without current cash; an increase in receivables or inventory uses cash relative to recognized earnings; an increase in payables postpones cash payment. Total cash change is −60, agreeing with closing140 minus opening200. Scoring: 1 operating flow; 1 investing/financing; 2 correctly signed bridge; 1 cash reconciliation.

    (d) Forgoing the early payment leaves 900 available now in exchange for owing1000 later: the supplier financing rate is 1000/900−1=1/9≈11.1111% for three months. The bank monthly rate is 24%/12=2%; its three-month effective rate is (1.02)³−1=0.061208=6.1208%. Repayment is 900(1.02)³=955.0872 USD. The effective annual rate is (1.02)12−1≈26.82418%, not24%. The 10% invoice discount uses1000 as denominator; the financing return on900 uses900. Scoring: 1 supplier rate; 1 monthly rate; 1 quarterly rate/repayment; 1 effective annual rate; 1 denominator distinction.

    (e) At the three-month date the equivalent costs are 945 USD for internal cash, because900 invested at5% would become945; 955.0872 USD for the bank; and 1000 USD for supplier financing. Internal cash is cheapest under the stated equal-risk/equal-feasibility assumptions, followed by the bank and supplier. Internal cash has foregone earnings of45 USD even though no lender sends an interest invoice. These are comparable date-three-month resource costs, not three new expenses in the earlier accrual statement. A liquidity restriction, tax, different risk or infeasible return could change the comparison. Scoring: 1 each equivalent cost; 1 ranking; 1 opportunity-cost explanation and scope.

  2. D2.

    (a) The feasible set is a nonempty triangle: it contains(0,0), is closed as an intersection of closed halfspaces, and is bounded by0≤x,y≤4. In finite-dimensional Euclidean space it is compact. The continuous polynomial f therefore attains a minimum. Its Hessian is diag(2,4), and for every nonzero v, vᵀHv=2v₁²+4v₂²>0; f is strictly convex. The feasible set is convex, so two distinct minimizing points would have a feasible midpoint with a strictly smaller value. Thus the minimizer is unique. Scoring: 1 nonempty/closed/bounded set; 1 compactness/continuity attainment; 1 Hessian; 1 positive curvature; 1 uniqueness argument.

    (b) With nonnegativity multipliers α,β≥0, stationarity is 2(x−4)+λ−α=0 and 4(y−3)+λ−β=0. The candidate x=2,y=2,λ=4,α=β=0 satisfies both equations. It is feasible, its resource sum equals4, and λ(x+y−4)=αx=βy=0. The loss is4+2=6 squared activity units. A global certificate follows in part(c), complementing the strict-convexity argument. Scoring: 1 equations/signs; 1 quantities; 1 multipliers; 1 feasibility/complementarity; 1 loss.

    (c) At b=4 and λ=4,

    L(x,y,4)=(x−2)²+2(y−2)²+6.

    The infimum over the retained nonnegative domain is attained at(2,2), so the dual lower bound is d(4)=6. Weak duality makes6 a lower bound on every feasible objective; the candidate attains6, certifying the optimum. At(1,3), f=9, and the primal–dual gap is3 squared activity units. It bounds objective excess f−V(4), here exactly3. A gap in loss units is not automatically a bound of3 activity units on distance or a claim about model realism. Scoring: 1 square completion; 1 domain minimum/dual value; 1 equality certificate; 1 gap; 1 error interpretation.

    (d) With the same λ but a new b, L=(x−2)²+2(y−2)²+22−4b, whose retained-domain minimum is22−4b. Hence V(b)≥22−4b. At b=0 only(0,0) is feasible, with V(0)=34, whereas the bound is22. At b=8 the unrestricted target(4,3) is feasible and yields V(8)=0, whereas the old bound is−10. Nonnegativity of f provides a sharper lower bound there. A valid fixed-multiplier bound can be loose; it does not state V(b)=6−4(b−4). The binding constraints and optimal multipliers can change with capacity. Scoring: 1 new dual expression; 1 bound; 1 zero-capacity optimum/value; 1 large-capacity optimum/value; 1 boundary/sensitivity distinction.

    (e) The equilibrium solves b*=2+b*/2, giving b*=4. Subtracting it gives bt+1−4=(bt−4)/2, hence bt=4(1−2−t) from b₀=0. Nonnegative starting capacity remains nonnegative; this path rises toward4. Absolute deviations shrink by1/2 each update, giving stability and convergence under the fixed rule. The tolerance condition is4·2−t≤1/8, or2t≥32, so the first date ist=5; t=4 still has error1/4. The constant update rule and its parameters must remain applicable; the calculation is not evidence that an actual capacity series obeys them. Scoring: 1 equilibrium; 1 path derivation; 1 stability/domain; 1 first date; 1 model condition.

  3. D3.

    (a) Pairs(0,2),(0,5),(0,9),(2,5),(2,9),(5,9) give means1,5/2,9/2,7/2,11/2,7 USD, each with probability1/6. Their sum is24, so expectation is4 USD, equal to the population mean. Centered squared deviations are9,9/4,1/4,1/4,9/4,9, summing23. The sample-mean variance is therefore23/6 USD². Scoring: 2 complete means/equal probabilities; 1 expectation; 1 squared-deviation total; 1 variance/units.

    (b) Each ordered draw is uniform over the four values. Its variance is [(0−4)²+(2−4)²+(5−4)²+(9−4)²]/4=23/2 USD². For two distinct ordered draws,

    E[X₁X₂]=[(0+2+5+9)²−(0²+2²+5²+9²)]/(4·3)=146/12=73/6.

    Thus covariance is73/6−16=−23/6 USD². The average has variance[2(23/2)+2(−23/6)]/4=23/6 USD². With independent replacement draws it would instead be(23/2)/2=23/4 USD². Without replacement, a large first value removes itself from the possibilities for the second, producing negative covariance. Scoring: 1 marginal variance; 1 cross moment/covariance; 1 reconstructed variance; 1 replacement comparison; 1 dependence mechanism.

    (c) The observed mean is7, the largest of the six possibilities. Its upper-tail null probability is1/6≈0.166667. Reject at0.20, but not at0.05. The next-highest possible mean is11/2, whose upper-tail probability is2/6>0.20, so the0.20 rule rejects only the largest pair and its actual null rejection probability is1/6. Discreteness makes the test conservative relative to0.20. This p-value is a tail probability under the fixed null sampling law, not the chance the null is true after observing the data. Such a posterior would require additional model probabilities and a Bayesian specification. Scoring: 1 tail calculation; 1 decision at0.20; 1 decision at0.05; 1 actual size; 1 interpretation.

    (d) Expected wealth is(9+25)/2=17 USD, and expected utility is(3+5)/2=4. Solving√[CE/(1 USD)]=4 givesCE=16 USD. The risk premium is17−16=1 USD. This decision maker is indifferent between the lottery and certain16, while a risk-neutral expected-wealth maximizer prefers the lottery's mean17. All final wealth levels are positive as required; expected utility and the utility of expected wealth are different calculations. Scoring: 1 mean; 1 expected utility; 1 CE; 1 risk premium; 1 both rankings/domain.

    (e) For signs(++),(+−),(−+),(−−), each with probability1/4, stopped gains are1,1,0,−2 USD, averaging0. The rule is admissible: the event of stopping at1 is determined by ε₁, and T≤2. Conditional mean-zero independent increments make M a martingale, so the result agrees with bounded optional stopping. Hindsight maxima are2,1,0,−1 USD, averaging1/2 USD. To choose time1 rather than2 by that rule requires knowing whether ε₂ is negative. That information is unavailable at time1, so the hindsight choice is not a stopping time for the natural information sequence. No fair-game theorem is contradicted. Scoring: 1 stopped outcomes; 1 stopped expectation; 1 admissibility/fairness; 1 hindsight outcomes/expectation; 1 future-information distinction.

  4. D4.

    (a) The original mean is(0+2+4+12)/4=9/2=4.5 USD. Small-group mean is2 USD; large-group mean is12 USD. The proposed target-weighted result is(1/4)2+(3/4)12=19/2=9.5 USD. It needs the target proportions and a justified assumption that the observed within-group means represent the target's corresponding group means. Reweighting cannot correct unmeasured selection within a group merely by fixing its overall share. Scoring: 1 overall mean; 1 each group mean; 1 weighted result; 1 transport/selection condition.

    (b) Tag counts2,1,1,3 create7 joined rows, with fees0,0,2,4,12,12,12. Their sum42 gives a naive mean6 USD. Joined small-group mean is6/4=3/2, while the large-group mean remains12. Applying target group proportions yields(1/4)(3/2)+(3/4)12=75/8=9.375 USD, still different from19/2. Duplication has changed weights within the small group; correcting only group totals does not repair that. Keep analytical records unique by firm ID, store tags separately or first collect all tags into one field per firm before a one-to-one join; reconcile counts and weighted totals afterward. Scoring: 1 joined count; 1 naive mean; 1 joined group means; 1 reweighted result; 1 grain diagnosis/repair.

    (c) Counts are(2,1,1), widths(3,3,9) USD, and density heights count/(4×width) are(1/6,1/12,1/36) per USD. Areas are(1/2,1/4,1/4), summing to one. The horizontal axis is fee in USD and the vertical axis is relative-frequency density per USD. This equal-firm display describes the four observed records, whose group shares are3/4 small and1/4 large; it has not applied the different target weights. Wide-bin counts alone should not be plotted as density heights. Scoring: 1 counts; 1 heights; 1 areas; 1 axes; 1 distribution target/width interpretation.

    (d) The original exact sum is1 cent; the stored values sum exactly to2 cents. The first conversion introduced a+1-cent error; the second input is represented exactly. Summing the represented values here introduces no further error. An exact or highly accurate summation routine given only those floats returns2, so it cannot recover the lost original information. Retain the original integer cents and sum them as integers, or preserve exact decimal/rational input before conversion. Exact arithmetic cannot establish that the ledger includes all intended transactions, uses the correct currency/sign/date, or avoids duplicate records. Scoring: 1 original sum; 1 stored sum; 1 error separation; 1 limitation/repair; 1 economic-data boundary.

    (e) In both models U=0 yields observed(D,Y)=(0,50), and U=1 yields(1,46), each with probability1/2. Model A has individual and average treatment effect−4 USD. Model B has Y(1)−Y(0)=6 for both U values, so its ATE is+6 USD. The predictor50−4D fits and predicts perfectly under either unchanged assignment law; held-out data from that same observable distribution cannot distinguish the models. Intervention changes D while holding the baseline U distribution fixed, revealing counterfactual outcomes never jointly observed for an individual. Here D=U also eliminates treatment overlap within U. A causal conclusion needs a justified design or additional counterfactual restrictions, not just better prediction. Scoring: 1 common observed distribution; 1 each ATE; 1 predictive equivalence; 1 intervention/identification explanation.

Method routes for remediation: opportunity cost, stocks, flows and statements, effective rates; constrained optimization, dual certificates, compactness, stable dynamics; covariance, sampling, exact inference, expected utility, bounded stopping; keys and joins, histograms, identification, predictive evaluation and exact numerical audits. This cumulative form samples these capabilities; it is not a claim to assess every topic in the four volumes.

Basic data-analysis practical — A repair desk's records and equipment choice

Format: open-resource individual analysis, 100 points in four essential domains of 25 points. Each domain has five parts worth 5 points. Allow roughly 3–5 hours for planning; this is an author estimate, not measured completion-time evidence. Use the accepted chapters, supplied files and standard-library Python. Advancement requires at least 85/100 and 19/25 in every domain, correction of critical errors, and the separate oral transfer. These are library design thresholds, not university rules or certification.

Every record and probability below is synthetic. The fictional repair desk has no actual customers, bank records or measured investment returns. April 2025 dates are invented scenario timestamps, preserved to test information availability. The case was authored on 7 October 2026 for the 6 October 2026 edition boundary. Your task is to make correct conditional calculations and explain their limits, not to present the result as evidence about a real firm.

Submit a short decision memo, a technical appendix answering the twenty parts, original inputs with their manifest, your executable analysis and preserved output, a discrepancy/test log and one independent calculation for each numerical domain. Freeze your first answers before comparing the instructor benchmark. A run of someone else's program without explanations does not complete the practical.

Inputs and execution

Download the record-level source snapshot, source notes and dictionary, hash manifest, benchmark program, preserved output and README. The program requires no installation, network connection or third-party package. Keep the three inputs beside it and run:

python3 foundation-practical-analysis.py
python3 -O foundation-practical-analysis.py
# Optional alternative input directory, with the same input filenames:
python3 foundation-practical-analysis.py /path/to/scenario

Inputs use integer USD cents; convert to USD exactly for the regression and investment calculations. Source hashes identify the authored input bytes relative to the manifest; they do not turn synthetic assumptions into empirical truth. Preserve the original package and make clearly named temporary copies for changes. No external data or source retrieval is necessary.

The observable ledger, operating versions and proposed investment

The ledger covers 7 April only. Opening stocks in USD are cash 2,000; receivables 300; equipment 1,000; supplier payables 200; loan principal 600; equity 2,500. There is no interest accrual, depreciation, tax, carried inventory, valuation change or other transaction in this deliberately small accounting model. Apply the stipulated recognition rules; no jurisdiction-specific accounting standard is being tested. The independent supplied statement reports closing cash of 2,630 USD.

A separate operations table measures daily variable consumables cost against scheduled jobs. It is not the whole company's daily operating expense, and these days do not belong to the 7 April ledger. Do not add the selected sample costs to that ledger. All six days are active. A day with zero jobs and a released zero cost is observed; a day without a cost release is missing.

The forecast origin is 8 April 2025, 12:00 UTC; the saved source snapshot is 12 April, 12:00 UTC. Features are committed scheduled job counts known at the listed time. Cost releases follow their observation day. Keep every revision. For training, choose the latest cost version available by the forecast origin. Fit the first four records only and freeze the resulting intercept OLS model for both future targets. At scoring, use a target's first cost release if available by the snapshot; leave unreleased targets unscored.

The equipment proposal is a separate, unexecuted decision at time 0 after the ledger closes. Its cash price is 500 USD. A purchase must leave immediate cash of at least 2,000 USD, with no new financing. The two later cash flows occur exactly one and two years after purchase. Use the stipulated effective annual nominal discount rate of 25%; all future amounts are nominal USD on the same price basis. This rate is an illustrative opportunity-rate assumption, not an APR, market quotation or empirical risk adjustment.

One state persists through both years. In the high state, probability 4/5, gross savings are 450 USD each year. In the low state, probability 1/5, gross savings are 250 USD each year. Using the space sacrifices 50 USD of rent at each year end. This is an incremental opportunity cost despite having no invoice in the historical ledger. No other cost, tax, salvage or terminal benefit occurs. Deferring produces zero incremental payoff in both states. Preferences are risk neutral; maximize expected discounted incremental USD subject to the cash reserve, and defer at an exact tie. These probabilities and savings are supplied assumptions; do not estimate them from the operating regression.

For a second representation of the decision, define statewise regret loss as the larger of buy's NPV and zero, minus the chosen action's NPV. These reported regrets compare both payoff alternatives before imposing cash feasibility; an infeasible purchase cannot be selected, whatever its unconstrained expected loss. Both the baseline and the 520-USD transfer below are feasible. Regret is measured in time-0 USD, distinct from a squared cost-forecast error in USD². Enumerate the two states before simulating. The optionality in this problem is choosing buy or defer before the state is revealed, not switching after seeing it.

D1 — Economic, financial and accounting reasoning (25 points)

  1. 5 points. Verify the opening balance-sheet identity. Classify the supplied opening/closing balances as stocks and the nine transactions as period events. State the units, entity, dates and exclusions needed for this reconciliation.
  2. 5 points. Compute operating cash flow, financing cash flow, total cash change and closing cash. Reconcile the latter to the supplied statement. Explain why borrowing, principal repayment and owner withdrawal do not belong in operating revenue or expense here.
  3. 5 points. Compute profit and every closing balance. Verify closing assets equal liabilities plus equity and reconcile profit with the cash change. Do not insert an unexplained balancing item.
  4. 5 points. Draw the investment timeline and calculate each state's annual incremental cash flows and NPV. Explain why the forgone rent belongs in this decision and why it was not an expense in the already closed ledger.
  5. 5 points. Check immediate purchase feasibility and the cash-price ceiling imposed by the reserve. Explain why the proposal does not change the supplied historical closing cash until executed. If hypothetically executed immediately, state the resulting cash and equipment asset exchanges, before any future earnings or depreciation.

D2 — Mathematical modeling and numerical reasoning (25 points)

  1. 5 points. Derive the origin-eligible simple intercept OLS fit from means and centered sums, or independently solve the two normal equations. State the coefficient units and the full-rank condition.
  2. 5 points. Give every fitted value and residual; verify both residual orthogonality identities. Compute SSE, TSS and R², with appropriate units. Explain why a zero residual sum does not establish causal exogeneity.
  3. 5 points. Holding the supplied state law and operating flows fixed, express expected NPV as a function of purchase price C. Prove its monotonicity, find the break-even price and combine it with the cash constraint. Interpret the tie rule at the boundary.
  4. 5 points. Holding price at 500, replace the high-state probability by p and the low-state probability by 1 − p. Derive the probability threshold for buying. Independently check one state's NPV by moving all its cash flows to year 2 and discounting the net advantage back.
  5. 5 points. In a clearly labeled changed-input scenario, increase the purchase price to 520 USD. Recompute feasibility, state NPVs, expected NPV and the optimal action. Preserve the original data and compare exact fractions before display rounding.

D3 — Probability, evidence and decisions (25 points)

  1. 5 points. From the two-state table, calculate expected purchase NPV, variance and standard deviation, and the probability of a negative NPV. Distinguish the risk of a single project from uncertainty in computing its expected payoff.
  2. 5 points. Give the full buy/defer regret-loss table and each action's expected loss. Show why its action ranking agrees with expected NPV in this case. State the assumptions supporting the decision.
  3. 5 points. Run 400 model replications with the supplied seed 40517 and integer-ticket state sampler. Report counts, simulated mean, error relative to the exact mean and estimated MCSE. Preserve the runtime and random-call rule. Do not make the action depend on a favorable simulated result.
  4. 5 points. Calculate the theoretical MCSE from the exact variance. Explain the replication unit and why drawing a fresh state separately each year changes the model. Distinguish the theoretical MCSE, estimated MCSE and payoff standard deviation.
  5. 5 points. Explain why more simulations do not validate the high-state probability, estimate a real firm's profitability or identify the machine's causal savings. State what extra empirical design/data would be needed. Explain why a single scored operating forecast does not support a reliable population prediction-error estimate or a confidence claim for a second, missing outcome.

D4 — Data, computation, timing and identification (25 points)

  1. 5 points. Produce the exact training-version table as of the origin. Explain why D1's zero is retained, D3 version 2 is excluded and D6 remains missing. Record the source snapshot, origin, units and hashes so the result can be reproduced.
  2. 5 points. Produce both frozen forecasts and score only outcomes available under the first-release scoring policy. State scored/unscored counts and MSE for the available subset. Identify which requested performance quantities remain unknowable.
  3. 5 points. For a diagnostic only, refit the same four training days using their latest versions at the saved snapshot. Give its coefficients and D5 prediction. Explain why a smaller D5 error obtained from this refit cannot retrospectively improve the original forecast.
  4. 5 points. Demonstrate one meaningful numerical discrepancy and three invalid-input failures in temporary copies. Use a changed loan receipt without changing the supplied bank cash; duplicate a day/version, insert a boolean monetary value and give a cost release preceding its observation day. Required checks must survive -O. Explain the limits of local hashes and a balance identity.
  5. 5 points. Write a concise recommendation that distinguishes the model decision, cash feasibility, statistical forecast, unreported outcome and causal claim. For an explicit transfer, suppose a new hypothetical D6 first cost of 18 USD were released on 12 April at 09:00 UTC. State what changes in scoring and what remains frozen. Do not insert that hypothetical value into the baseline.

Scoring, methods and critical errors

Each numbered part is worth 5 points. The instructor guide gives specific numerical targets and splits the points between calculation and interpretation. Equivalent correct derivations receive full credit. D1 is economic/accounting discipline; D2 mathematical derivation and exact checks; D3 probability and justified decisions; D4 auditable data/timing and reporting. A complete file submission is required for execution credit. Reserve conclusions about real institutions, statistical calibration and causality unless their required evidence is supplied.

Critical errors requiring repair include missing-as-zero imputation, a future revision used at the origin, counting a loan as revenue, mixing cents and dollars or USD and USD², changing simulation seeds to obtain the preferred action, treating model probabilities as estimated facts, or claiming that the OLS slope identifies causal cost. Repair the failure and explain a changed-case check before advancement even if the total score exceeds 85.

Accepted method routes: opportunity cost, stocks and balance sheets, present value, linear systems, moments, preferences and decisions, provenance, Monte Carlo, projection, identification, prediction timing and numerical audits. This practical reuses taught methods; no new external empirical source is being asserted.

Complete instructor answers and per-part scoring

D1 answers

  1. Opening assets are 2,000 + 300 + 1,000 = 3,300 USD; liabilities 200 + 600 = 800; equity 2,500. Thus 3,300 = 800 + 2,500. Balances are dated stocks; receipts/payments and recognition events occur during 7 April. Inputs are cents and displayed values USD for the single synthetic desk. No omitted tax, interest, depreciation or valuation entry is to be invented. Score: identity 2; dates/stock-flow/units 2; exclusions and entity 1.
  2. Operating cash is 200 + 600 − 400 − 100 = 300 USD. Financing cash is 500 − 50 − 120 = 330; investing cash is zero. Total change 630 and closing cash 2,630 match the statement. Borrowing raises cash and debt; principal repayment reduces both; withdrawal reduces cash and equity. None is operating revenue/expense under the supplied rules. Score: flows 2; closing/reconciliation 1; classifications 2.
  3. Profit = 900 − 400 − 150 = 350. Receivables close at 300 − 200 + 900 − 600 = 400; equipment 1,000; payables 200 + 150 − 100 = 250; loan 600 + 500 − 50 = 1,050; equity 2,500 + 350 − 120 = 2,730. Assets are 2,630 + 400 + 1,000 = 4,030; liabilities plus equity are 250 + 1,050 + 2,730 = 4,030. Operating cash = profit − Δreceivables + Δpayables = 350 − 100 + 50 = 300; add financing 330 to obtain the 630 cash change. Score: profit/receivables/payables 2; remaining balances/identity 2; cash-profit bridge 1.
  4. Time 0 pays −500. Each high-state year gives 450 − 50 = 400; each low-state year gives 250 − 50 = 200. Discount factors are 4/5 and 16/25, summing to 36/25 = 1.44. High NPV is −500 + 400(1.44) = 76 USD; low NPV −500 + 200(1.44) = −212. Forgone rent is a consequence of committing the space; the historical ledger contains no executed proposal or future sacrificed receipts. Score: timeline/net flows 2; discounted NPVs 2; opportunity-cost scope 1.
  5. Immediate post-purchase cash would be 2,630 − 500 = 2,130, above the 2,000 reserve. The cash-price ceiling is 630. The observed historical statement remains 2,630 because the purchase is only proposed. If executed, cash falls 500 and equipment rises 500 to 1,500, an asset exchange; total assets and equity initially remain unchanged under the specified model. Later earnings/depreciation require their own records. Score: feasibility/ceiling 2; unexecuted scope 1; hypothetical asset exchange 2.

D2 answers

  1. Eligible x = (0,1,2,3), y = (0,4,4,10) USD. Means are x̄ = 3/2, ȳ = 9/2. Sxx = 5 and Sxy = 15, giving slope 3 USD/job and intercept 0 USD. Equivalently the normal equations are 4a + 6b = 18 and 6a + 14b = 42; determinant 20 > 0 gives uniqueness. At least two distinct x values make the intercept and x columns independent. Score: sums/equations 2; coefficients 2; units/rank 1.
  2. Fits are (0,3,6,9), residuals (0,1,−2,1) USD. Their sum is zero; weighted sum is 0 + 1 − 4 + 3 = 0. SSE = 0 + 1 + 4 + 1 = 6 USD²; TSS = 20.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 30.25 = 51 USD². R² = 1 − 6/51 = 15/17. Orthogonality is an algebraic property of this fitted projection; it does not establish a population disturbance independent of job scheduling or a counterfactual treatment comparison. Score: fits/residuals 1; identities 1; sums/R² 2; scope 1.
  3. Expected annual net benefit is (4/5)400 + (1/5)200 = 360 USD. Thus E[NPV(C)] = 360(36/25) − C = 2,592/5 − C = 518.4 − C. Its derivative with respect to USD price is −1, so it strictly decreases; the NPV constraint is C ≤ 518.4 for weak nonnegativity. Cash feasibility requires C ≤ 630. The tighter bound is 518.4; at equality the specified tie rule defers, so strict positive-NPV purchase requires C < 518.4 within the feasible range. Score: expected-value function 2; monotonicity 1; both bounds/tie 2.
  4. E[NPV] = 76p − 212(1 − p) = 288p − 212. Buy if p > 212/288 = 53/72, provided cash is feasible; defer at equality. At p = 4/5, this inequality holds. In the high state the year-2 advantage is 400(1.25) + 400 − 500(1.25)² = 118.75 USD at year 2. Discount by 1.25² to recover 76 USD at time 0. The low-state equivalent is −331.25/1.5625 = −212. Score: threshold derivation 2; tie/feasibility 1; independent timing calculation 2.
  5. At C = 520, cash is 2,110 and remains feasible. State NPVs fall by exactly 20 to 56 and −232. Expected NPV is 18.4 − 20 = −1.6 = −8/5 USD, so defer. This is a price sensitivity, not a new probability estimate or altered historical cash statement. Score: feasibility 1; state values 1; expectation/action 2; preserved baseline/interpretation 1.

D3 answers

  1. Expected NPV = (4/5)76 + (1/5)(−212) = 92/5 = 18.4 USD. For a two-point law, variance is p(1 − p)(76 + 212)² = 331,776/25 = 13,271.04 USD²; standard deviation 576/5 = 115.2 USD. A single purchase loses in the low state, probability 1/5. This payoff dispersion persists even when the expectation is computed exactly. Score: expectation 1; variance/SD with units 2; loss probability 1; risk-versus-computation 1.
  2. High-state regret: buy 0, defer 76. Low-state regret: buy 212, defer 0. Expected regret is 212/5 = 42.4 USD for buy and 304/5 = 60.8 for defer. Their difference is 18.4, favoring buy, just as expected NPV does. Subtracting each action's payoff from the same statewise best payoff preserves the ranking after expectation. The probabilities, incremental payoffs, risk-neutral criterion and feasible reserve are assumptions; no claim of optimality under unspecified risk aversion follows. Score: loss table 2; expected losses/ranking 2; assumptions 1.
  3. On the recorded CPython 3.14.6 run, initialize one rng = Random(40517), then make 400 successive rng.randrange(5) calls. Tickets 0–3 mean high and 4 means low, producing high 327 and low 73. The mean is [327(76) − 73(212)]/400 = 586/25 = 23.44 USD; error relative to the exact mean is +5.04. With sample variance s² = Σ(vᵢ − v̄)²/399, estimated MCSE is √(s²/400) ≈ 5.569053051 USD. Record the generator, call order and runtime; higher-level random routines can vary across versions, so a documented different stream should still reconcile its own counts and moments. The exact model, not this run's sign, determines the benchmark action. Score: reproducible stream/counts 1; mean/error 2; estimated MCSE 1; decision/portability scope 1.
  4. The theoretical MCSE is 115.2/√400 = 5.76 USD. Each replication is one complete two-year project with one persistent state. Drawing a new independent state for each year changes covariance and hence project variance, even though its mean might remain unchanged. Payoff SD 115.2 describes one project's dispersion; theoretical MCSE 5.76 describes repeated 400-project model averages; estimated MCSE 5.569053051 uses this run's sample variance. At 1,600 independent complete-project replications the theoretical MCSE would halve to 2.88. Score: theoretical calculation 1; correct replication/dependence 2; distinction among dispersions 2.
  5. More model draws approximate stipulated expectations more precisely but supply no evidence that p = 4/5 or savings 450/250 describe reality. Estimating these inputs requires relevant data and a justified sampling/model procedure; a causal machine-effect claim additionally needs defined treatment, outcome, unit and a credible counterfactual design, with assumptions such as consistency and no interference where appropriate. The four training costs were not generated by an identified machine experiment. One available forecast error is descriptive of D5; the missing D6 error is unknown and a population accuracy interval has no supplied sampling/design justification. Score: simulation-versus-input evidence 2; causal requirements 2; sparse/missing-score limit 1.

D4 answers

  1. The origin uses D1 v1 released 2 Apr 09:00, D2 v1 released 3 Apr 09:00, D3 v1 released 4 Apr 09:00 and D4 v1 released 5 Apr 09:00, all UTC. D1 is a measured zero and remains in the fit. D3 v2 is released 11 April, after the 8 April origin; being present in the saved 12 April snapshot does not make it historically available.   2. The frozen fit predicts D5 12 USD and D6 15 USD. D5's first cost 15 is released by the scoring snapshot, so actual-minus-forecast error is 3 USD and squared error 9 USD². D6's actual, error and loss remain null, not zero. Scored count 1, unscored count 1, available-subset MSE 9 USD². The two-target MSE and D6 error are unidentified from this snapshot. Forecasts at job counts 4 and 5 also extend beyond the training support 0–3; a fitted line supplies the extrapolation, not a guarantee.   3. Latest training y becomes (0,4,8,10). The later descriptive refit has intercept 2/5 = 0.4 and slope 17/5 = 3.4 USD/job. At x = 4 it gives 14 USD, a D5 error of 1 instead of 3. It uses the 11 April revision and therefore cannot be called a forecast made on 8 April. Its better retrospective error is not valid untouched evaluation of the original information set.   4. For example, changing L7 from 500 to 510 increases calculated closing cash to 2,640, while supplied bank cash remains 2,630: discrepancy +10 USD.
